analysis.one_liner: Bars discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity under the nation's core civil rights laws.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on the Equality Act, so it never came to a Senate vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Equality Act would amend the Civil Rights Act, Fair Housing Act, and Equal Credit Opportunity Act to explicitly ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity — and make clear that sex discrimination includes pregnancy and sex stereotypes. It would also broaden the definition of "public accommodations" to cover stores, online services, health care providers, shelters, and transportation, and would bar religious-liberty claims under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being used as a defense to discrimination under these laws. The bill had all 48 Democratic senators and both independents backing it, but was referred to the Judiciary Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBTQ Americans and women gain explicit, nationwide protection against discrimination in employment, housing, credit, schools, federally funded programs, public accommodations, and jury selection. Because federal law currently protects sexual orientation and gender identity clearly only in employment (under Bostock), the biggest gains are in housing, credit, public accommodations, and services — areas where the bill's findings document pervasive discrimination, including against transgender people in shelters and foster placement.

how_it_helps.text: It writes sexual orientation and gender identity into the core federal civil rights statutes alongside race and sex, so discrimination against LGBTQ people is illegal nationwide in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations, education, and jury selection.

It expands 'public accommodations' beyond hotels and restaurants to include any establishment providing goods, services, or programs — stores, shelters, health care, online retailers, and transportation services — closing gaps in the 1964 law.

It prohibits denying anyone access to a restroom, locker room, or dressing room consistent with their gender identity, and bans using the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense to discrimination claims under the covered laws.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses, landlords, lenders, and federally funded organizations bear new anti-discrimination obligations and expanded legal liability. Religious individuals and organizations that object to serving LGBTQ people, including some adoption and foster care providers, lose a potential defense under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act.

drawbacks.text: The bill specifies that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 cannot be used as a claim or defense under the statutes it amends, removing a shield that religious objectors — including some faith-based schools, shelters, and adoption agencies — have relied on.

The bill requires access to restrooms, locker rooms, and dressing rooms in accordance with gender identity, and expands 'public accommodations' to cover essentially any business offering goods, services, or programs — including online retailers and health care providers — which critics argued reached further than the 1964 law's original scope.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for LGBTQ people and women are concrete and well documented in the bill's own findings. The principal cost is to religious individuals and organizations who object to serving same-sex couples or accommodating transgender people in shared facilities, and the bill removes the RFRA defense that might otherwise have shielded them — the sharpest good-faith objection to the bill and the likely reason it could not reach 60 Senate votes. Expanding public accommodations to online services and health care is broad and will generate litigation over its edges.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it never came to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 23, 2021, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and no further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended.
It had 48 cosponsors — every Senate Democrat and both independents — but no Republican cosponsors.
Because it stayed in committee, the Senate never debated or voted on the bill, and it died when the Congress expired on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses, landlords, lenders, and religious objectors who wanted to keep deciding whom to serve remain free to do so; LGBTQ people and women keep no new federal protection from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Businesses and religious objectors to the rules

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on February 23, 2021.

for.name: 46 of 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of 2 independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, representing the entire Democratic caucus plus both independents.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, and as the chamber's majority under the filibuster rules they could have brought it to the floor; none did.

against.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
against.what_they_did: Was the only Democrat to publicly state he would not vote for the bill as introduced, leaving it short of the 60 votes needed to break a filibuster.

sides.party_line_note: Every Senate Democrat and both independents cosponsored the bill; not a single Senate Republican did, and the bill never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Employers and businesses serving the public
industries.note: The bill barred all covered businesses from discriminating by sexual orientation and gender identity, and sharply expanded which businesses count as 'public accommodations' (including online services and health care). Compliance obligations and litigation exposure grow, though many large employers already followed these policies voluntarily.

industries.industry: Religious organizations and faith-based service providers
industries.note: The bill extended anti-discrimination rules to religiously affiliated providers of goods, services, housing, and adoption placement, and barred the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being used as a defense under the covered laws. This is the industry the bill most directly constrains.

The Equal Credit Opportunity Act's sex-discrimination ban would explicitly cover sexual orientation and gender identity, plus discrimination based on association or inaccurate perception, in mortgage, credit card, and student lending decisions.
